about.label: About
about.heading: Wachirathan Waterfall — A Natural Jewel of Doi Inthanon
about.lead: One of the most powerful and photogenic waterfalls on the road to Doi Inthanon's summit
about.paragraph1: Wachirathan is a single-drop waterfall about 80 metres high, fed by the Mae Klang (Huay Mae Klang) stream, a tributary of the Ping River. It sits at kilometre 21–22 of the Chom Thong–Doi Inthanon summit road (Highway 1009) inside Doi Inthanon National Park, Chiang Mai.
about.paragraph2: A short walk from the car park brings you close to the falls, with wooden bridges and viewing platforms. The misty base often throws up rainbows when the sun hits the spray, while a nature trail leads into the lush rainforest around the waterfall.
about.quote: When sunlight strikes the spray, Wachirathan glitters like scattered diamonds.

highlights.title: A single giant drop
highlights.desc: A ~40 m-wide curtain of water plunges ~80 m in one drop, its roar echoing through the forest

highlights.title: Rainbow mist
highlights.desc: Morning spray often forms rainbows — a favourite for photographers

highlights.title: Nature trails
highlights.desc: Shady paths through rainforest, great for birding and botany

editorTip.text: Park at the upper lot and walk down — you'll reach the closest, quietest viewpoint

eco.label: Ecology
eco.heading: High-Mountain Rainforest & Microclimate
eco.quote: The endless plunge shapes not only the falls, but a thriving 'mist micro-ecosystem' in the gorge.
eco.intro: Wachirathan sits in a valley at about 750 m above sea level within Doi Inthanon National Park. Water from the Mae Klang stream (แม่กลาง) drops 80 m onto a granite wall; the impact shatters it into suspended mist, creating a naturally humid microclimate zone.

micro.title: Extreme humidity
micro.desc: Even in the Northern dry season (Nov–Apr), relative humidity within 100 m of the falls stays above 90%.

micro.title: Natural cooling
micro.desc: Mist evaporation draws away heat, keeping the area 3–5°C cooler than the city below — a cool, damp local pocket.

micro.title: Oxygen-rich air
micro.desc: Tumbling water releases negative ions, making it Doi Inthanon's natural high-mountain 'oxygen bar'.

plants.title: Mosses & epiphytes ('hanging garden')
plants.desc: Rock faces and trunks in the densest mist wear a thick emerald carpet of bryophytes.

items.name: High-mountain ferns
items.desc: Bird's-nest fern (Asplenium nidus), staghorn fern and climbing ferns draped on trunks

items.name: Native dendrobium & orchids
items.desc: Wild orchids on old branches bloom in turn between rainy and cool seasons, feeding on the humid air

plants.title: Shade-loving undergrowth
plants.desc: Along the boardwalk in moist humus soil grow diverse high-mountain shade plants.

items.name: Wild ginger & begonias
items.desc: Begonias (Begonia) with patterned leaves and native ginger brighten the forest floor

items.name: Wild banana & balsam
items.desc: Banana thickets along the stream shelter small animals

plants.title: Evergreen broadleaf canopy
plants.desc: The ridge above is cloaked in evergreen trees of Lauraceae and Fagaceae whose overlapping crowns filter harsh direct sun for the layers below.

eco.wildlifeTitle: 3. Highland Life on the Food Chain
wildlife: Birdwatching haven: the crimson sunbird (Aethopyga siparaja), blue whistling thrush, white-capped redstart and kingfisher along the stream
Amphibians & insects: mossy banks are breeding grounds for mountain toads, tree frogs and rare damselflies (stream jewelwings)
eco.lntIntro: The micro-ecosystem is extremely fragile — trampled moss and epiphytes can take years to recover.
lnt: Stay on the boardwalk and viewpoints; never step on the moss and vegetation outside the path
Do not pick wild orchids or plants — leave them whole for wildlife and later visitors
Carry out all your rubbish so nothing pollutes the high-mountain stream water

history.label: History
history.heading: The Name & Story of Wachirathan
history.intro: The name 'Wachirathan' comes from Pali–Sanskrit roots, hinting at the sparkling beauty of its spray

blocks.title: What 'Wachirathan' means
blocks.text: 'Vachira' (Sanskrit vajra) means diamond or thunderbolt; 'thara' means stream. Together they mean 'Diamond Stream' or 'Thunderbolt River' — likening the sparkling spray to scattered diamonds.

blocks.title: Former name: 'Tad Kong Yong'
blocks.text: Before becoming widely known as Wachirathan, locals called it 'Tad Kong Yong' (Tard Klong Yong), after the stream that feeds it from Doi Inthanon.

blocks.title: Part of Doi Inthanon
blocks.text: The area around the falls lies within Doi Inthanon National Park, established in 1972 and home to Thailand's highest peak.

blocks.title: From royal forest to national park
blocks.text: Long before it became a national park, the Doi Inthanon massif was a protected royal forest (ป่าสงวนพระเจ้า) and a favoured retreat of the Lanna court. In 1954 it was designated a forest park, and on 2 October 1972 — as Thailand's 6th national park — it was formally opened to the public under the name Doi Inthanon National Park.

legend.title: Local Legend
legend.text: Local lore says a naga spirit dwells in the deep pool, guarding the clear water. Elders say that if you speak softly, the spray forms curious shapes they call the 'waterfall's diamonds'.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: The falls flow all year round, fed by the Mae Klang stream from Doi Inthanon, so they never run dry even in the hot season.

stories.title: Named after the Thunderbolt
stories.text: Legend says that Lanna-era monks passing through heard the falls roar like a vajra (thunderbolt) striking stone on stormy nights, with spray scattering like diamonds — so they named it after the Sanskrit word “Vajra”, believing the place was guarded by divine power.

stories.title: The Naga's Deep Pool
stories.text: Villagers believed a Naga serpent spirit guarded the deep pool at the base of the falls. When the rainy season swelled the water, elders would warn children not to play in the pool, out of respect for the water spirit.

stories.title: A Royal Summer Retreat
stories.text: In the Lanna kingdom era, Doi Inthanon was a favoured summer retreat of the royal court. The forest around the falls was formally designated a protected forest in 1954, laying the groundwork for the national park established in 1972.

photography.title: Photography & Rainbow Guide
photography.intro: Plunging 80 m with an intense high-pressure mist, Wachirathan is one of the easiest places in Northern Thailand to capture a 3-D double rainbow and silky long-exposure water. Master the light angle and you'll get postcard shots.

times.desc: The golden rainbow window. Sunlight hits the base mist and a clear — often double — rainbow arcs over the lower viewpoint.
Fewest crowds, soft light. Misty forest glow — perfect for slow-shutter silky water streaks.
Sun drops behind the ridge; the falls fall into shade and the rainbow fades, but light is even for deep rainforest mood shots.

spots.name: Lower main viewpoint
spots.view: Head-on to the full fall — rainbows most often arch across the mist right in front of you.
spots.tip: Use an ultra-wide (16–24mm); place a person at the rail as foreground for a 'human + rainbow + giant fall' frame.

spots.name: Upper side wooden bridge
spots.view: Avoids the heaviest mist; shows splash detail on the rock face and dense high-mountain ferns.
spots.tip: Use the bridge lines as leading lines to the mid-fall; shoot vertical to stress the 80 m height.

spots.name: Bottom stream & rocks
spots.view: Away from crowds; mossy boulders make great foreground.
spots.tip: Low angle near the water; let the stream's converging lines pull the eye, contrasting flowing water with still rock.

settings.camera: Shutter 1/4s–2s · f/8–f/11 · ISO 100 · tripod + ND filter (ND8/ND64)
settings.phone: iPhone: shoot Live Photo then choose 'Long Exposure'. Android: Pro mode, shutter 0.5s–1s.
Normal photo mode; tap the brightest part of the rainbow to focus and expose.

tips: Waterproofing first: the mist is like artificial rain — you're soaked in 10 seconds at the main viewpoint.
A CPL polariser is the rainbow cheat: it kills glare on wet rocks, boosts green saturation, and strengthens rainbow contrast.
Three-step shoot: set up away from the mist; cap the lens and walk in; wipe the glass, compose, fire, then retreat under cover.
Bring 3–4 microfibre cloths (one gets soaked fast), a rain cover for the camera, and an absorbent towel.

bestTime.title: Best Season & Flowering
bestTime.intro: At about 750 m above sea level, Doi Inthanon is cooler than the plains. Water volume and scenery shift through the year — plan by season for a smoother trip.

seasons.name: Steady flow · Best morning mist
seasons.desc: Groundwater stored from the rains keeps the fall flowing year-round; cool-season water is steady and clear. Mornings often wear a thin veil of mist and the temperature is pleasant (~15–25°C) — the most comfortable season for families and seniors.

seasons.name: Slightly less water · Shady & cool
seasons.desc: Flow eases a little from the cool season but stays impressive; midday is hot, so go early or late. The altitude's shade and mountain breeze feel cooler than the plains.

seasons.name: Max flow · Mind the slip
seasons.desc: Heavy rain makes the falls most powerful and the mist thickest, with frequent rainbows. But trails get slippery and hillsides may shed rocks — wear grippy shoes and watch the weather alerts.

items.title: No swimming
items.desc: Swimming in the deep pool at the base of the falls is strictly prohibited — currents and submerged rocks are dangerous

items.title: Slippery trails
items.desc: Boardwalks and steps get very slippery in the rainy season (Jun–Oct); wear proper footwear and hold the rails

items.title: Stay on paths
items.desc: Keep to marked viewpoints and trails; the cliff edges near the falls are steep and unstable

accessibility.title: Accessibility & Senior Tips
accessibility.intro: Wachirathan is fairly friendly for families and seniors: the walk from the car park to the main viewpoint is short and gently graded, with well-built boardwalks and rails.

items.title: Gentle boardwalk
items.desc: The boardwalk from the car park is nearly flat, with continuous handrails along the way — wheelchairs and strollers can reach the lower viewpoint.

items.title: Close to the falls
items.desc: Just a few minutes' walk from the car park brings you to the main viewpoint, so no long trek is needed — easy even for seniors.

items.title: Facilities
items.desc: Car park, toilets and food stalls are near the entrance. Avoid the midday peak in high season; early morning or late afternoon is more relaxed.

items.name: Sirithan Waterfall
items.desc: A slender 40 m fall a few km north, fed by the Mae Klang — a quiet photo stop

items.name: Mae Ya Waterfall
items.desc: One of the park's largest falls, a multi-tier curtain of water ideal for a longer hike

items.name: Phra Mahathat Chedi
items.desc: The twin pagodas (Naphamethinidon & Naphaphonphumisiri) near the summit, built to honour the royal family

faqs.q: Does the waterfall flow all year?
faqs.a: Yes — fed by the Mae Klang stream from Doi Inthanon. The rainy season (Jun–Oct) brings the most powerful and photogenic flow.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: Rainy season for full flow; cool season (Nov–Feb) for pleasant weather and soft light. Mornings bring mist and rainbows.

faqs.q: Is it a long walk to the falls?
faqs.a: No — just a few minutes' walk from the car park to the main viewpoint, with ramps and wooden bridges.
Yes — car parks, food stalls, souvenir shops and toilets are near the entrance.
The falls are inside Doi Inthanon National Park, so the park entrance fee (see above) applies.

weather.heading: Current Weather & 7-Day Forecast
weather.lead: The valley microclimate at the falls often differs from the city below. Check the live conditions before you go — whether to bring an umbrella, and how warm to dress, all in one view.

weather.umbrellaMaybe: Possible showers — pack a light rain jacket just in case
weather.umbrellaNo: Low chance of rain — travel light; still consider non-slip shoes for the mist zone

facilities.label: Visitor Services
facilities.heading: Facilities & Nearby Services
facilities.lead: An overview of the types of services commonly found at the falls and nearby, so you can plan with confidence. We do not recommend specific businesses; actual availability may vary on site.

items.title: Restrooms
items.desc: Public restrooms are located near the entrance and parking areas; some are Thai-style squat toilets — bring your own tissue and hand sanitiser.

items.title: Parking
items.desc: Two large parking areas (upper and lower) sit close to the viewing trail entrances; they fill up on holiday afternoons, so arrive in the morning.

items.title: Food & Drink
items.desc: Local snack stalls and simple food stands operate near the parking area in high season, serving affordable northern Thai favourites; bringing your own snacks also works.

items.title: Accommodation
items.desc: There is no lodging at the falls themselves. Chom Thong town and the Doi Inthanon road offer a range of stays, from family guesthouses to resorts.

items.title: Shops & Supplies
items.desc: A small kiosk at the falls sells drinks and snacks; do your main shopping in Chiang Mai city or Chom Thong town beforehand.

items.title: Fuel & Charging
items.desc: The mountain road adds up quickly — refuel in town before heading up. EV drivers should plan charging stops ahead, as charging points inside the park are limited.

items.title: Medical & Emergency
items.desc: The national park visitor centre can assist with basic needs; serious cases require the Chom Thong hospital. Mobile signal can be patchy in the mountains — stay alert.

items.title: Connectivity
items.desc: Signal is good at the main viewing areas but may weaken deeper on the trails. Download offline maps for navigation.

facilities.note: As a non-profit educational site, this overview describes facility types only and is not affiliated with any business.

plans.label: Tailored Plans
plans.heading: Visit Plans by Traveller Type
plans.lead: Three targeted routes: families with kids / photography & nature / low-mobility accessible. Pick the one that matches your group and follow it directly.

groups.title: Family with Kids
groups.desc: Relaxed pace, safety first, shortest walking distances, with fun nature learning.
schedule: 08:30 Arrive at the lower car park; start with photos from the viewing deck
09:00 Walk the wooden bridge to the base of the falls (about 20 min return)
10:00 Read the interpretive signs at the nature-trail entrance — mosses and ferns
11:00 Simple lunch at the stalls by the car park
tips: Pack a change of clothes for kids — the mist zone soaks everything
Guardrails line the whole route, but keep children from climbing over

groups.title: Photography & Nature
groups.desc: Chasing light — rainbows, long exposures and macro nature windows.
schedule: 06:40 Arrive at golden hour; shoot light shafts piercing the mist at low angles
08:30 Front-lit panorama of the main falls; try 1/4s silk-water long exposures
10:00 Macro walk on the nature trail — mosses, ferns and wild orchids
16:30 Return for side-lit evening shots and reflections at the base
tips: Keep a lens cloth ready — mist coats the glass in 3 minutes
Yield to pedestrians when tripod-mounted on the bridge

groups.title: Low-Mobility / Accessible
groups.desc: Shortest walking, fewest steps — comfortable for visitors with limited mobility and their companions.
schedule: 09:00 Park at the upper car park — only a few steps from the viewing deck
09:15 Enjoy the full panorama from the railed viewing deck; gentle slopes only
10:00 Rest and take photos at the seating area beside the deck; return anytime
10:30 If energy allows, descend to the wooden bridge (steps involved — optional)
tips: The upper-car-park route is essentially step-free; wheelchairs can reach the viewing deck
Restrooms are next to the car park with a short, flat path

itinerary.label: Suggested Routes
itinerary.heading: Recommended Itineraries
itinerary.lead: Two ready-made routes — half-day and full-day — that work on their own or chained with other Doi Inthanon sights.

routes.title: Classic Half-Day (about 3.5 hours)
steps: 08:30 Arrive at the upper car park; first shots from the viewing deck
09:00 Wooden bridge to the base of the falls — mist and rainbows up close
10:00 Loop the nature education trail and learn the rainforest plants
11:00 Simple lunch at the stalls, then head back or onward

routes.title: Deep-Dive Full Day (about 7 hours)
steps: 07:00 Early arrival; golden-hour light on the main falls
08:30 Full nature education trail — birding and macro photography
11:00 Lunch and rest at the car park area
13:00 Drive to Sirithan Waterfall (about 10 minutes away)
15:00 Continue up to the summit and the twin chedis
17:00 Watch the sea of clouds from the top, then descend

conservation.label: Science & Stewardship
conservation.heading: Conservation & Visitor Responsibility
conservation.lead: Wachirathan's ecology rests on a fragile, mist-fed microclimate. Understanding it is the first step to protecting it.

points.title: Mist is Life
points.desc: Humidity within 100 m of the base stays above 90% all year; mosses and epiphytes depend on it and take years to recover once trampled.

points.title: The Stream Food Chain
points.desc: The Mae Klang stream flows from the falls to villages downstream — water quality directly affects farms and aquatic life, and pollution travels down the chain.

points.title: Home of Montane Birds
points.desc: Sunbirds, thrushes and kingfishers breed here. Keep your distance when birding — no flash, no playback calls.

points.title: Natural Air-Conditioning
points.desc: Mist evaporation keeps the area 3–5°C cooler than the city. This cooling depends on intact vegetation — litter and trampling weaken it.

dos: Stay on the boardwalks and designated platforms
Carry your rubbish out — leave no trace
Keep your voice down; do not disturb wildlife
Follow park rules; on-site notices prevail if anything changes
donts: Climb over railings into the mist zone
Pick orchids or trample mosses for photos
Use detergent in the stream or leave food scraps
